title: What is the SIR Costing?
shows: The Wire's column puts the Election Commission's budget for 2026-27 at Rs 382.20 crore, Rs 367.99 crore of it for elections, and says the Commission's funds are routed through the Ministry of Law and Justice, which has Rs 250 crore for voter ID cards this year, while the states pay for the booth level officers and the machinery of the revision. It cites the Telangana Chief Electoral Officer's estimate of Rs 200 crore for the revision in the state, Rs 85 crore of it for booth level officers and other staff, Ei Samay's report that a West Bengal budget of Rs 450 crore was exceeded, and the Sabar Institute's estimate that electors in West Bengal spent Rs 1,983 crore on travel, food and lost work to attend hearings. It says no figure has been published for what the revision cost in Delhi.
quote: For the financial year 2026-27, the ECI has been allocated Rs 382.20 crore, a 25.33% increase from the Rs 304.98 crore it was allocated last year.
According to the Telangana Chief Electoral Office, the estimated cost of SIR in Telangana is going to be Rs 200 crore. Of this, Rs 85 crore is for BLOs and other officers deployed in this exercise.
The institute calculates this out-of-pocket expenditure for people in this entire exercise to come to a total of Rs 1,983 crore.
note: By Kavita Kabeer, whom The Wire describes as a writer and satirist, published 1 November 2026 at 4:35 pm IST (post_date_gmt 11:05:23), read in full through The Wire's CMS API (posts/detail) with curl on 3 November 2026. The Wire's page title is 'What is the SIR Costing?' and its address carries an earlier headline. The column gives no source for the Telangana estimate beyond the Chief Electoral Office, and the Sabar Institute's estimate is not among the Sabar pieces already on the reading list. It also cites The Indian Express for a cost of thousands of crores for each national cycle and the West Bengal government's releases of Rs 51 crore and Rs 38.8 crore for booth level officers. Not carried: its count of names taken off the rolls, which mixes names left off the drafts with names deleted, its statements on welfare schemes in West Bengal and Bihar, its account of individual electors, and its political comment on the Union government and the Law Minister.
